title: Run a process pool from a real script and collect results
sources: Python 3.14 Standard Library: concurrent.futures ProcessPoolExecutor/Future.result, multiprocessing spawn and safe importing of main module; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Processes, multiprocessing, pickling constraints, pools, IPC, CPU-bound work
whyItMatters: A pool of processes can work on independent CPU-heavy tasks, but unlike a thread pool it must start worker interpreters and transfer job/result data. Errors must return to the caller visibly.
simpleExplanation: Each worker process has its own Python interpreter and ordinary memory. ProcessPoolExecutor starts a bounded pool, serializes an importable function plus arguments to a worker, and returns a Future. Calling future.result() gives the value or raises the worker's exception in the parent. On Windows, workers use a fresh interpreter; put pool startup under if __name__ == '__main__' in a saved script so importing the module does not recursively start workers. A lambda or nested function is not a portable pool callable. The small example below uses the explicit spawn start method to test this rule across platforms. It illustrates IPC through pool arguments/results, not shared memory or a browser Python runner. Process startup and serialization have costs; benchmark a realistic CPU workload before claiming speedup.
mentalModel: The parent is a dispatcher. It posts a small work order to another office, receives either a result or a failure report, and must close the offices when done. The offices do not share the parent's desk contents.
outcomes: Place a worker function at module top level and guard startup.
Submit picklable independent inputs to a bounded ProcessPoolExecutor.
Retrieve each Future result and handle an expected worker error.
Explain why this saved-script example is not a browser/REPL lab or proof of speedup.

realWorldExample.scenario: A local course analytics tool scores independent batches of practice results.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: An interactive-only lambda fails to reach workers; an ignored Future hides an invalid batch; copying huge data for tiny jobs erases any performance benefit.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Use a top-level pure scorer, small validated payloads, bounded workers, explicit result/error collection, a saved script entry point and workload-based measurements.

explanation: score_points is at module top level, so a spawned worker can import it; the tuples and integer results are small and serializable.
The main guard prevents imported worker modules from starting a new pool again.
Submitting all jobs returns Futures; future.result() is where worker results or exceptions become visible to the parent.
The with block closes the pool. max_workers=2 bounds worker count, but this tiny workload is a correctness demo, not a performance benchmark.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Save the code as a .py file and run it with Python. Try a larger valid tuple, but measure end-to-end time before claiming a speedup. The in-site guided lab can inspect and edit code; actual spawned-process execution needs a local script runner.

procedure: Put a pure worker at module top level and define small serializable job/result records.
Save the entry point in a real .py file; guard pool creation under if __name__ == '__main__'.
Use a bounded ProcessPoolExecutor and submit independent jobs.
Read every Future.result, report expected validation failures and let unexpected failures surface.
Measure startup, serialization and full workload time against a sequential baseline before choosing processes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Launching a process pool while a module is imported.
commonMistakes.why: Spawned workers import the main module and may recursively start more processes.
commonMistakes.avoid: Guard the entry point in a saved script.

commonMistakes.mistake: Submitting a local closure, lambda or open resource.
commonMistakes.why: The worker must import/deserialize the callable and input; these choices are not portable payloads.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use a top-level function and small plain-data arguments.

commonMistakes.mistake: Submitting work but not reading Futures.
commonMistakes.why: A worker exception can be missed and the report may look complete.
commonMistakes.avoid: Call result on every Future and distinguish expected from unexpected errors.

lab.title: Complete a guarded two-worker scoring script

simulation.prompt: A spawned worker imports process_pool_demo.py. Which top-level code should run automatically in that worker?
choices: The score_points function definition only; guarded main() is skipped
The guarded main() call creates another pool
Future.result() runs before any job is submitted
simulation.explanation: The worker imports the module, so top-level definitions become available. The __main__ guard prevents the worker import from launching another pool.

lab.safety: Fictional local scoring only; no network, files other than the learner's saved script, or untrusted pickle data. The site shows editable guided practice, but browser execution cannot spawn OS processes; run this lab as a saved .py script in a local Python environment.

lab.solutionExplanation: A spawned worker imports the guarded script, runs only the top-level scorer and returns values or an error through the Future. The script-based companion file in this lesson directory was tested on Windows; this exercise still requires the learner's local Python rather than claiming in-browser OS process execution.
challenges: Predict what would happen if pool creation moved to module top level under spawn.
Find the blind spot if the code never calls future.result().
Experiment with a sequential baseline and report full elapsed time rather than assuming this tiny workload is faster in a pool.

projectConnection.milestone: Prototype a guarded local process worker for independent CPU-heavy scoring and record per-batch outcomes.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: A saved script runs on the target OS, every Future is inspected, invalid batches are visible, and end-to-end benchmarking determines whether multiprocessing is worthwhile.

assessment.question: Why guard process-pool startup with if __name__ == '__main__'?
assessment.answer: Spawned workers import the module; the guard prevents recursive startup.
assessment.explanation: This is especially important on Windows and with spawn.

assessment.question: Where does a process worker's error become visible to the parent?
assessment.explanation: Ignoring a Future can hide failed work.

assessment.question: Does this small pool example prove processes are faster than sequential code?
assessment.explanation: Startup and serialization overhead require representative end-to-end measurement.
